overview: Champa was a string of Cham kingdoms along the coast of what is now central Vietnam, first recorded by the Chinese as Lin-yi in 192 CE. Seafarers and traders, the Chams built brick towers to Shiva and fought the Khmer and the Vietnamese for more than a thousand years.

items.text: Brick tower temples at My Son, built from the seventh to the thirteenth century, with sandstone carving of a fineness that rivals Angkor.
Sandstone images of Shiva, Vishnu, Ganesha and dancing apsaras in the Cham styles of Tra Kieu and Dong Duong.
Cham ports sold agarwood, ivory, gold and cinnamon to China and the archipelago and sheltered ships waiting for the monsoon.
Cham sailors traded and raided across the South China Sea and up the Mekong; they sacked Angkor in 1177.
Shaivism was the royal cult, with Buddhism strong at Dong Duong in the ninth century; Islam reached the Chams from the fifteenth century.
Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions record kings and gifts to temples; the Dong Yen Chau stone of the fourth century is the oldest text in any Southeast Asian language.
My Son Sanctuary was listed by UNESCO.
Cham communities in Vietnam and Cambodia keep the language and, in Cambodia, Islam.

fall.text: The Vietnamese took the capital Vijaya in 1471; the last Cham principality, Panduranga, was absorbed by the Nguyen emperor Minh Mang in 1832.
